content.title: About
content.content: Zucchini is a young fruit of the summer squash (Cucurbita pepo), typically green. The fruit is eaten raw with its skin, preserving most of its nutrients. Zucchini is popular in salads, smoothies, and fresh dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Zucchini belongs to the gourd family and is a variety of summer squash.
There are more than 50 cultivars, differing in shape and skin shade.
Unlike many vegetables, zucchini is about 95% water.
Both skin and flesh are edible, so peeling is unnecessary.
Zucchini is often spiralized into “zoodles” as a pasta substitute.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and folate are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cucurbits.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic zucchini, wash it thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Storing at room temperature for too long can allow bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Zucchini can be eaten raw in salads, thinly sliced in smoothies, or used in wraps. The skin is tender and nutritious, so no peeling is needed. Optionally, sprinkle with a little salt and let sit 10‑15 minutes to draw out excess moisture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store zucchini in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container; it stays fresh for up to 5 days. Keep it away from ethylene‑producing fruits to slow ripening.
